$comment: R1770 — `$at` above is the SURFACE EXTENT this document's canon was
written against, and it is first because it governs how the rest is read.
Until that round no pin in this tree named a size, and this file is the
case that showed what it costs: the screen's own gate held 2494x1531 as a
private constant inside its test module, while the assembled tool gives
the same section a page of 1388x848 and judges what it draws there against
this same file. Below 1601 wide that screen declares it stops laying out
and clips instead, so the two gates were reading two different builds
through one document and neither artifact said so. The screen's gate now
reads the number from here.
R1732 — the analysis tool's NODE INSPECTOR, written down once, in neutral
vocabulary, as the behaviour reference draws it.
WHY THIS IS A FILE AND NOT A RUST CONSTANT. The reason the two spec files
beside it are, applied to a third surface. The screen's own `spec` module
is what a RUNNING screen needs — paint tags, row data, the wording of a
refusal. A specification written there would be written by the same hand in
the same edit as the thing under test, so a conformance check would be
asking the subject for the answer.
EXTRACTION. The reference is not in this repository and must not be. The
procedure is the recorded one: the document is a single JSON string line
holding the whole application as one inline script, and the inspector is
one block of markup fed by one derivation. Measured 2026-08-19: the
derivation gives each field FIVE mutually exclusive control kinds, and the
markup draws exactly one of them per row, in the order recorded below. The
row's header line carries the path, a type word that appends how many words
are on offer when the field has a roster, one badge saying when an edit
lands, and a seat that takes the row away when it is the reader's to take.
THE ENUMERATION ROW IS WHAT THIS ROUND IS ABOUT. The reference draws it as
a COLLAPSED control carrying the word the row holds and an arrow that opens
the rest — styled identically to the text field beside it, so the two read
as the same kind of thing. This build drew every option side by side until
R1732: measured, a six-word roster overran its own control by 50px and a
seven-word one by 113px, with no wrap, no clip and no scroll.
VOCABULARY. The reference's product, protocol and resource words are
replaced by the words the tool class uses generally. Structure and
behaviour are what is being reproduced; the wording is not. The titles
below are this file's words for what is drawn — the reference labels almost
none of these parts — and the file says so rather than pretending otherwise.
THE TWO HALVES. Each surface carries `canon` — what the reference has — and
`owed` — where this build differs, each entry carrying the round that
accepted it and why. The gate asserts the difference between the built
surface and `canon` is EXACTLY `owed`, so a new divergence fails and so
does an owed one that has been paid off without this file being told.
OWED RUNS IN BOTH DIRECTIONS. A part this build has and the reference does
not is a divergence too, and is recorded here rather than deleted: the
standing order rule is that the reference is what must be REPRODUCED and
not a ceiling, so something present here and absent there stays and says
why.
★★★★★ R1742 — TWO OF THESE SURFACES ARE ALTERNATIVES, and this file could
not say so. Measured, not designed: the round that made the running screen
publish its verdict asked this document about a live frame for the first
time, and `enum_row` came back with an eighth part. The reason is written
three paragraphs down in `enum_row`'s own comment — the row is specified
WITH ITS ROSTER SHUT, because a roster standing over it is a part of the
row that is not always there. So the row and the roster cannot both be on
screen, and the screen now answers `away` for whichever one is not, naming
the state.
The consequence is worth stating where the pin is rather than leaving it
to be re-derived: THIS DOCUMENT CANNOT BE FULLY JUDGED AT ANY ONE INSTANT.
A reader who wants the whole verdict drives the session and reads twice.
That is not a defect in the report — it is what `the verdict is about a
session` means when a session has states that exclude each other — but it
does mean `reconciles()` is never true here, and the type has no way to
distinguish `not opened yet` from `cannot stand beside its sibling`. Only
the screen's away sentence says which, and a sentence is not machine
readable. Recorded as `debt-a-document-cannot-say-two-surfaces-are-
alternatives`, with the three alternatives that were considered and not
taken.
★★ R1742 — AND `controls` IS JUDGED AGAINST THE FORM ON SCREEN. Its own
comment below says the build's side is read from `a form holding one row of
each kind`, which is a session and not a property of the build. Measured in
the assembled tool at rest, the card it opens on draws only some of the
kinds fixed here, so the rest report absent and the ordering shifts around
them — read the ledger below for which, rather than a count written here,
because that count went stale the first time the card's rows changed
(R1842). True about that card, and it reads as a claim about the build. The
reading that would fix it is refused
on purpose: an away-condition of `the form does not hold a row of every
specified kind` is an escape hatch wide enough to swallow the mechanism,
because a painter drawing an enumeration as a row of chips (the defect
R1732 repaired) would take that kind off the surface and the surface would
then decline to be judged. Deciding it from the FIELD SHAPES rather than
from the classification would be sound and independent, and the hook that
answers has no model to read. So the number stands and the caveat is
written here.
The kinds of value control the inspector draws, in the order the
reference's markup tests for them. Exactly one is drawn per row, and
which one is a function of the field's declared type — the reference says
so in a comment of its own on that derivation.
A build's side of this is read back from the PAINT: a form holding one row
of each kind is laid out and each row is classified by the affordances
actually drawn inside its control. A table of intentions would pass while
the painter drew something else.

owed.sentence: part 3 `perm` (one chip per permission word, each on or off) is specified and the surface has no such part
owed.why: ★★★★★ The reference draws ONE control over a set of named booleans, and this screen stopped asking for one. R1842 moved the option surface off this crate's memory of the target and onto the target's own declaration, which declares the two permissions as SEPARATE boolean leaves and holds them as an object of booleans. The single set-valued row this screen had was keyed at a path that is not a leaf at all and composed an ARRAY there, so what it exported was a document the target refuses — and refuses loudly, since a wrong type stops it starting where an unknown key only warns. Two boolean rows are correct and this control is what they cost. It is NOT abandoned: a field shape that authors a set of named booleans as an object is on the common-widget-catalog axis's remainder (`python3 tools/phase_b_tally.py --owed`), and when it exists this entry is paid off by putting the row back.

owed.sentence: `derived` is specified at part 4 and sits at part 3
owed.why: The consequence of the entry above and nothing else: `perm` is specified between `bool` and `derived`, so a surface missing `perm` has `derived` one place earlier. Declared separately rather than folded into it because the two are different facts — one part is absent and one part is in the wrong place — and a ledger that let an absence excuse an ordering would stop noticing an ordering defect that had no absence behind it.

owed.sentence: part 4 `int` is on the surface and no specification declares it
owed.why: A second-pass improvement, kept deliberately. The reference draws a whole number in the plain text box — its text-kind list names the numeric types — so a value outside the range the configuration accepts is typed in and refused later. R1651 gave the shape its bounds and R1652 gave it a stepper that clamps, so the control cannot leave the range at all. The standing order rule keeps what the reference lacks. (The ordinal in the sentence moved at R1842 with the `perm` row; the difference itself is unchanged.)

owed.sentence: part 5 `list` is on the surface and no specification declares it
owed.why: The same, one kind over. The reference draws an array of addresses as one comma-separated text box, so a person editing the third element counts commas. R1652.1 gives a list one row per element and a row that appends one. Kept for the same reason. (Ordinal moved at R1842 with the `perm` row.)

$comment: The roster the collapsed control opens, in the order the configuration
offers the words — which is the reference's order too: it maps the
field's own option list and marks the one equal to the value.
The words are the routing-mode roster this tool's option surface declares.
They are the specification's here because the surface being reproduced is
an ordered one: a roster that quietly reordered itself would move the
option under a reader's finger between one opening and the next.
EACH TITLE IS THE WORD ITSELF, and that is the reference's own
construction rather than a shortcut here: it draws each option with its
value as the option's text, so what a row is CALLED and what it is
ADDRESSED BY are one string. The build's side reads the title back out of
the run painted inside that option's box, so a roster whose third row drew
the second word fails — which a key-only comparison could not see.
★★★★★ R1842 — AND THE WORDS CHANGED, BECAUSE THEY WERE THE WRONG ONES.
Until this round the roster held the three SESSION MODES, which is what
a node comes up as; the row is about how a node ROUTES, and the two are
different keys with different vocabularies. The mistake was invisible
while the option surface was written from this tree's memory of its
target — the row's key was a paraphrase, so nothing could be asked which
words it takes. Read from the target's own declaration, the routing row
offers two: every node talking to every other, and a computed map of the
links. The reference's own screen offers exactly those two on that row.
What the words mean, for a reader of this file rather than for the gate:
peer-to-peer is every node talking to every other, and linkstate is each
node routing over a map of the links it has been told about.
